strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: sequential risk monitoring of deployed models under scarce labels. The proposed PPRM framework cleanly generalizes supervised risk monitoring (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2021) to the semi-supervised setting by integrating PPI/PPI++ estimates, which is a natural yet non-trivial combination.

The theoretical treatment is careful about the key subtlety: the adaptive reliance hyperparameter η_t must form a predictable sequence to preserve unbiasedness of the prediction-powered estimates (Lemma 3.1), and this is what enables the assumption-free false-alarm guarantee of Theorem 3.2. The plug-in estimator (27) with sliding windows respects this constraint.

The false-alarm guarantee is assumption-free and finite-sample, avoiding the calibration-type assumptions required by unsupervised alternatives (Schirmer et al., 2025; I Amoukou et al., 2024); requiring only nt > 0 labeled samples per step is a meaningful relaxation.

Experiments cover three distinct domains (image classification on CIFAR10-C, LLM monitoring with LLM-as-a-judge imputation across multiple predictor scales, and a wireless channel-equalization task), including a self-synthetic variant where the deployed model itself imputes labels. Results consistently show earlier alarms than SRM while preserving validity, and URM's failure to alarm is a useful contrast.
The ablation on fixed vs. adaptive η_t (Table 1) is informative, showing that adaptive selection matters most for weaker imputation models, which is the practically relevant regime.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core results are direct adaptations of existing tools: Lemma 3.1 is a straightforward linearity-of-expectation argument, Theorem 3.2 'follows directly from Lemma 2.2', and Lemma 3.3 is explicitly the PPI++ variance-optimal solution (Angelopoulos et al., 2023b, Example 6.1). The contribution is an instantiation of PPI within the Podkopaev-Ramdas framework rather than a new methodology. The relationship to prediction-powered e-values for sequential change detection (Csillag et al., 2025) deserves deeper differentiation.

Empirical gains are modest. Improvements in time-to-alarm over SRM are on the order of 3-10% (e.g., 760 vs. 800; 500 vs. 530; Table 1 shows ~2-4% gains from adaptivity). Given the added complexity of an auxiliary predictor, unlabeled data pipelines, and η_t estimation, the practical benefit needs stronger justification; no statistical significance analysis or multiple-seed variance quantification beyond full-range error bars is provided.

Several presentation and consistency issues: notation inconsistencies between (17)/(33)/(34) (the η_0 coefficient on the unlabeled term appears and disappears; f_0 vs. f); Section 5 says 'two case studies' while three are presented; the abstract claims 'extensive experiments' for what is a small number of settings; Appendix B contains a garbled sentence merging Assumption 1's statement into the surrounding text.

Missing ablations that would strengthen the evidence: sensitivity to the labeled-to-unlabeled ratio (only 1:15 is tested), sensitivity to δ = δS + δT, behavior when the imputation model is adversarially poor, and the effect of the clamping at η_max on the optimal-η theory (note η*_t in (26) can be negative when Cov(ut, ũt) < 0, and constraining η ≥ 0 breaks the claimed variance optimality).
Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several experimental details (number of runs, how labeled samples arrive, hyperparameter search for baselines) are under-specified.

No dedicated limitations section. Practical constraints—e.g., the need for a strictly positive labeled stream at every step, the cost of obtaining synthetic labels from an LLM judge at scale, and the restriction to bounded losses—are acknowledged only obliquely or left to future work.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important problem: monitoring deployed ML models under harmful distribution shifts when ground-truth labels are scarce and costly. The semi-supervised framing is well-motivated (Section 1, Figure 1).

The proposed PPRM framework is technically coherent: the key observation that the PPI tuning parameter ηt can be chosen as a predictable sequence (Lemma 3.1) while preserving unbiasedness is correct and is exactly what is needed to combine PPI-style estimators with anytime-valid confidence sequences (Lemma 2.1, CM-EB), yielding the false-alarm guarantee in Theorem 3.2.

The core methodological move — enforcing predictability of the adaptive hyperparameter via a sliding-window plug-in estimator (27)-(28) — is a clean and correct way to retain statistical validity while adapting reliance on unlabeled data online.

Evaluation spans three reasonably diverse domains (CIFAR10-C image classification, LLM QA monitoring with multiple imputation models, and a wireless channel-equalization task in Appendix C.3), including a self-synthetic setting where the deployed model supplies its own labels, and comparison against supervised (SRM), unsupervised (URM), and idealized baselines.
The paper is clearly written, with a well-structured problem formulation (Section 2) that faithfully reproduces the Podkopaev & Ramdas setup before generalizing it.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the contribution is essentially the assembly of existing tools — PPI/PPI++ estimators (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a,b) inserted into the supervised risk-monitoring framework of Podkopaev & Ramdas (2021) with the CM-EB confidence sequence (Howard et al., 2021). All three theoretical results are direct corollaries of prior work: Lemma 3.1 is PPI++ unbiasedness plus conditioning on a predictable ηt; Theorem 3.2 'follows directly from Lemma 2.2' (the authors' own words); Lemma 3.3 is explicitly identified as 'the same as Example 6.1 of PPI++'. The paper also sits very close to anytime-valid PPI (Kilian et al., 2025) and prediction-powered e-values for sequential detection (Csillag et al., 2025); the claimed differences ('different hypothesis, different experimental setup') are asserted but not convincingly demonstrated, e.g., no head-to-head comparison against these closely related approaches.

The reported gains are modest and the experimental configuration is permissive: with δ = δS + δT = 0.25, the method tolerates up to a 25% probability of false alarm, which is arguably impractical for a safety-oriented monitoring system (typical budgets would be 0.01–0.05). Detection-time improvements over SRM are small in several settings (e.g., ~760 vs ~800 in Figure 2(b); ~500 vs ~530 in Figure 3; ~498 vs ~519 in Table 1), and the margin to Ideal PPRM remains large, leaving the practical value of the extra machinery unclear.

The proof of the source-risk upper bound (Appendix A.2) is hand-wavy: the per-block quantities z^PP_{0,i} are constructed, the Waudby-Smith & Ramdas betting algorithm is invoked, and validity is concluded with the phrase 'the resulting bound is naturally valid.' The z^PP_{0,i} depend on the data-dependent block pairing and on η0, and their boundedness/range (needed for the betting bounds) is not verified; a rigorous argument is missing. Relatedly, the affine normalization ga(·) in Section 3.2 is described for the lower bound but the interaction with the upper bound (and with ηmax) is not fully specified.

Statistical dependencies that the theory assumes are not discussed in relation to the experiments: the guarantee requires the labeled and unlabeled streams to be independent and drawn from the same Pt at each time, and requires the i.i.d. batch structure; in the LLM experiment, the 'complex prompts' are constructed by filtering on another model's failures (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), which induces a selection mechanism whose interplay with the i.i.d. assumption is not analyzed. No experiment probes robustness when these assumptions are violated (e.g., correlated labeled/unlabeled batches, non-i.i.d. arrival).

Reproducibility concerns: the number of independent runs/seeds behind the 'full range' error bars is never stated; no code release or repository is mentioned; several experimental details (choice of window L, n0/N0 in the calibration set, how the 'risk threshold' R0 + εtol is set in each task) are under-specified.

The abstract advertises 'LLM monitoring via an LLM-as-a-judge,' but the experiments actually monitor QA accuracy using synthetic labels from stronger LLMs; the LLM-as-a-judge methodology (Zheng et al., 2023) is cited but not genuinely instantiated, so the abstract oversells this aspect.

No limitations section or honest discussion of the method's scope: e.g., dependence on nt > 0 labeled samples at every time step, sensitivity to the quality of fp(·) in the small-predictor regime (Table 1 shows ~80-step degradation), and the computational cost of the CM-EB supremum computation at every step. The impact statement is boilerplate.

Baseline treatment is uneven: URM fails to alarm in the main image experiment and is then dropped from several subsequent comparisons (Figures 3, 5(a), 7); the strongest and most recent related methods from the testing-by-betting line (Xu et al., 2024; Timans et al., 2025) are discussed in Related Works but not compared, even in a variant form.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely practical gap between supervised risk monitoring (SRM, which requires many labels) and purely unsupervised monitoring (URM, which requires hard-to-validate calibration assumptions), namely the semi-supervised regime where labeled data exist but are scarce while unlabeled data are abundant.

The core technical idea is clean: because prediction-powered risk estimates remain unbiased whenever the PPI hyperparameter sequence {ηt} is predictable (Lemma 3.1), the anytime-valid false-alarm guarantee of Podkopaev & Ramdas carries over essentially unchanged (Theorem 3.2), while allowing the online variance-optimal choice of ηt from PPI++ (Lemma 3.3). This is a tidy and correct way to retain assumption-free finite-sample validity while exploiting unlabeled data.

The evaluation covers three meaningfully different domains (CIFAR10-C image classification, LLM QA monitoring with LLM-as-a-judge imputation, and a wireless channel-equalization task), includes the self-synthetic setting where the deployed model itself provides labels, and ablates predictor strength and fixed vs. adaptive ηt. Results consistently show earlier detection than SRM, and URM fails to alarm in some settings, supporting the practical value of the approach.

The paper is generally well written and clearly motivated, with the monitoring problem, hypotheses, and guarantees (PFA control, expected time to alarm) formally defined, and honest positioning against SRM/URM and testing-by-betting alternatives.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely a combination of existing components: PPI/PPI++ estimators (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a,b), conjugate-mixture empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences (Howard et al., 2021), the SRM monitoring framework (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2021), and betting-based upper bounds (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, 2024). The novel proofs (Lemmas 3.1, 3.3 and Theorem 3.2) are short, direct adaptations of prior results, which limits conceptual novelty.

Empirical gains are modest. Detection-time improvements over SRM are on the order of a few percent (e.g., alarm at t≈760 vs. t≈800 in Fig. 2; t≈500 vs. t≈530 in Fig. 3), and the reported false-alarm budget is loose (δ = δS+δT = 0.25). The practical significance of these deltas relative to the added machinery (a separate predictor, extra unlabeled data, and adaptive ηt estimation) is not fully established.

Baseline coverage is narrow. The closest related method, the prediction-powered e-value approach for sequential change-point detection (Csillag et al., 2025), is dismissed in a single sentence as differing in hypothesis and setup; an empirical comparison, or at least a precise discussion of why it is not applicable, would strengthen the claims. No code release or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned.

There are presentation/notation issues that reduce polish: eq. (17) uses f0 for both the deployed model and the labels produced by the predictor fp, which is inconsistent with eq. (18) and the general formulation; Lemma 2.1 contains leftover notation (γ defined but superseded by δT) and the statement appears garbled relative to the original theorem; several proofs are deferred with a 'directly follows' style rather than complete derivations.

The framework requires strictly positive labeled data (nt > 0) at every time step, which the authors acknowledge distinguishes them from unsupervised methods but which narrows applicability; behavior under label droughts or when labeled batches are skipped is not analyzed or tested.

The sliding-window plug-in estimator of ηt (27) is evaluated under non-stationary distributions where the optimal ηt itself drifts; the paper does not quantify how window length L or lag in the estimate affects tightness of the bound in practice, and there is no limitations section discussing these choices, the choice of δ split, or sensitivity to L, n0/N0, and ϵtol.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—monitoring deployed models when labels are scarce—and proposes a clean semi-supervised extension of supervised risk monitoring (SRM) via prediction-powered inference (PPI), generalizing Podkopaev & Ramdas (2022) to streams with both labeled and unlabeled batches.

The statistical guarantees are rigorous and well-structured: Lemma 3.1 establishes unbiasedness of the prediction-powered running-risk estimator for any predictable sequence of reliance parameters ηt, and Theorem 3.2 inherits assumption-free anytime-valid type-I error control from the SRM framework. The predictability requirement is handled carefully via a sliding-window plug-in estimator (27).

The adaptive selection of ηt via variance minimization (Lemma 3.3 / PPI++-style optimal η) is a sensible and empirically validated addition, with the ablation in Table 1 and Figures 12–13 showing that adaptivity prevents degradation with weak predictors.

Experiments span three domains (image classification on CIFAR10-C, LLM QA with LLM-as-a-judge imputation, and a wireless channel-equalization task), including a self-synthetic setting where the deployed model itself imputes labels, and the empirical false-alarm curve in Figure 5 empirically validates the type-I error guarantee.

The appendix contains a thoughtful approximate detection-delay analysis (Proposition A.1) that clarifies the trade-off between variance reduction and the range-normalization penalty (1+2η)², plus an extension to intermittent label streams that interpolates between supervised and unsupervised monitoring.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely a composition of existing techniques—PPI/PPI++ variance-optimal imputation, CM-EB anytime-valid confidence sequences (Howard et al., 2021), and the SRM decision framework of Podkopaev & Ramdas (2022)—so the methodological novelty is incremental. The relationship to concurrent prediction-powered e-value approaches for sequential testing (Csillag et al., 2025) is discussed but the comparison is only conceptual.

Empirical gains over SRM are often modest: e.g., alarm times of ~760 vs ~800 (Figure 2a), ~760 vs ~790 (Figure 2b), and ~500 vs ~530 (Figure 3), with overlapping inter-run variability in the box plots. No statistical significance analysis of the detection-delay differences is provided.

The baseline set is thin: comparisons are against SRM, URM (Schirmer et al., 2025), and an idealized oracle, but the unsupervised method of Amoukou et al. (2024) and betting/e-value based sequential change detectors (Shekhar & Ramdas, 2023) are not empirically compared despite being discussed as related alternatives.

The setting requires at least one labeled sample at every time step (nt strictly positive), which is a practical limitation for the motivating 'labels are costly' narrative; this is acknowledged implicitly (Section 3.1) but its implications and the labeling-cost trade-off are not analyzed in the main text, and there is no explicit limitations section.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several experimental details (number of trials, exact shift constructions, how LLM prompt shifts are sampled per trial) are underspecified relative to the level of detail needed to replicate Figures 2–5.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated: monitoring deployed models with scarce labels is practically important, and the paper positions itself clearly against SRM (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2022), purely unsupervised monitoring (Amoukou et al., 2024; Schirmer et al., 2025), and the PPI literature.

The core idea of inserting prediction-powered estimates into an anytime-valid sequential test is natural and, to the authors' credit, appears genuinely unexplored for this monitoring problem; requiring n_t > 0 to obtain assumption-free guarantees relative to Schirmer et al. is a sensible design choice.

The main theoretical claims (Lemma 3.1 unbiasedness with predictable η_t, Theorem 3.2 type-I error control) are stated cleanly, and the predictability requirement on the hyperparameter sequence is handled correctly, including via the sliding-window plug-in estimator (27).

Experiments span three modalities (image classification, LLM-as-a-judge QA monitoring, wireless channel equalization), include both external-predictor and self-synthetic settings, and evaluate sensitivity to predictor accuracy, window length, abrupt vs. gradual shifts, and intermittent label streams. The empirical false-alarm trajectory in Figure 5 is a meaningful validation of the guarantee.
The delay analysis in Appendix A.4 (Proposition A.1) honestly characterizes when PPRM helps, including the range-normalization penalty (1+2η)^2, rather than claiming universal improvement.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Theorem 3.2 is essentially Lemma 2.2 applied to unbiased estimates, Lemma 3.3 is explicitly the PPI++ Example 6.1 solution, and the confidence machinery is taken verbatim from Howard et al. (2021) and Waudby-Smith & Ramdas (2024). The contribution is a combination of known components; the derivations in Appendices A.1–A.3 are routine.

A possible soundness gap around the affine normalization: the correction term w_t^PP is derived on the [0,1]-normalized scale (Section 3.2, Appendix A.4), yet the decision rule (23) compares the unnormalized quantities L_t^PP > U_0^PP + ε_tol without stating the required rescaling of the correction terms (or of ε_tol) back to the original scale. This should be made precise, as it affects whether the stated type-I guarantee holds as written.

Appendix A.2's construction of the source upper bound is hand-wavy: the per-block statistic z_0,i in (35) does not lie in [0,1] (it ranges roughly over [-η0, 1+η0] in aggregate terms), and the claim that 'the resulting bound is naturally valid' by directly invoking the betting algorithm of Waudby-Smith & Ramdas is not justified; the formal validity of the union-bound argument δ = δ_S + δ_T for this mixture of bounds is not fully proven.

The error budgets are permissive: δ = 0.25 total (δ_T = 0.2, δ_S = 0.05) for the main experiments, and Figure 5 refers to a target δ_T = 0.15 that is inconsistent with the stated δ_T = 0.2. A 15–25% allowance on false alarms is generous for a safety-monitoring method, and the paper does not report results at stricter (e.g., 5%) levels.

Empirical gains over SRM are modest: alarm times improve from ~800 to ~760 (Fig. 2a), ~790 to ~760 (Fig. 2b), and ~530 to ~500 (Fig. 3), with overlapping variance bands in several panels. Given that PPRM additionally requires an auxiliary predictor and 15x more unlabeled data per step, the cost-benefit case is not compelling.

The i.i.d.-within-time-step assumption conflates the labeled and unlabeled streams at each t (both drawn from P_t); in real deployments, labeled samples are typically collected through a different, selective acquisition process (e.g., human review of flagged cases), which would break the unbiasedness argument in Lemma 3.1. This limitation is not discussed.
No code or implementation details sufficient for reproduction are provided; reproducibility of the LLM experiments (specific prompts, label extraction, judge protocols) is particularly unclear.

The harm-detection framing carries safety implications (deciding when to halt or retrain a deployed model), yet the limitations discussion is thin — e.g., behavior when the auxiliary predictor degrades under the very shifts being monitored is only addressed indirectly in Appendix D.3.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem — monitoring deployed models under distribution shift with limited labels — and proposes a clean, well-motivated semi-supervised extension of supervised risk monitoring (SRM) via prediction-powered inference (PPI).

The theoretical core is sound: Lemma 3.1 (unbiasedness of the PPI risk estimate under a predictable sequence of hyperparameters) is correct and is the key ingredient allowing adaptive eta_t without breaking the anytime-valid guarantees; Theorem 3.2 then follows rigorously by combining this with the union bound over the source upper bound and the CM-EB lower confidence sequence, yielding assumption-free finite-sample type-I error control without requiring calibration assumptions on the imputation model (unlike purely unsupervised baselines).

The adaptive procedure for selecting the reliance parameter eta_t (Lemma 3.3 / Eq. 27) is a sensible plug-in of the PPI++ variance-optimal solution, with the predictability requirement correctly handled via a sliding-window estimator, so statistical validity is preserved.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad and well designed: image classification (CIFAR-10-C), LLM monitoring with several LLM-as-a-judge predictors (including a self-synthetic variant), and a telecommunications channel-equalization task. Notably, the paper validates the type-I error guarantee empirically (Figure 5, cumulative false-alarm rate below target), studies predictor-accuracy effects, abrupt vs. gradual shifts, window-length sensitivity, and intermittent label streams (Appendix D), all of which strengthen the evidence beyond a single demo.

The comparison includes a meaningful baseline set (SRM, URM from Schirmer et al., and an idealized full-label upper bound), which allows the reader to gauge how much of the achievable gap PPRM closes.

Appendix A.4 provides a useful (if heuristic) detection-delay analysis, including a condition (Proposition A.1) making explicit when PPRM beats SRM, which clarifies that gains depend on predictor informativeness versus the range-normalization penalty.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the contribution is essentially a careful composition of existing components — PPI/PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al. 2023a,b) inserted into the SRM framework of Podkopaev & Ramdas (2022) with CM-EB confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021) and a betting-based source bound (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2024). Theorem 3.2 is a direct corollary of Lemma 3.1 and existing SRM machinery; Lemma 3.3 is explicitly a restatement of PPI++ Example 6.1. The combination is natural and useful, but the conceptual novelty is limited.

The introduction overstates the variance benefit: it claims PPRM 'produces tighter confidence bounds than SRM' in general, whereas the paper's own analysis (Proposition A.1, Appendix D.3) shows gains are conditional on predictor quality and that fixed-eta PPRM can even underperform SRM with a poor predictor. The main text should state this conditionality upfront.

The detection-delay theory in Appendix A.4 is heuristic, relying on large-t approximations (Eq. 42) that are not justified rigorously; Proposition A.1 is an 'approximate' condition, and the connection to the empirical results (Figure 6) is only numerical.

Minor but real inconsistencies and gaps: the target error budget is stated as delta_T = 0.2, delta_S = 0.05 in Section 5, but Figure 5 reports target delta_T = 0.15; Appendix A.2's block-wise pairing for the betting-based source bound assumes N0/n0 is an integer and introduces an ad hoc pairing construction whose validity (exchangeability of the blocks) is asserted rather than proven; Lemma 3.1 implicitly requires labeled and unlabeled samples at time t to share the same conditional risk distribution, which deserves explicit statement.

The scale and realism of the experiments are somewhat limited: batch sizes of 1 labeled and 15 unlabeled samples per step, synthetically constructed shifts (Gaussian corruption schedules, prompts filtered by another model's failures), and a small number of tasks. There is no discussion of how performance would behave under more complex label-scarcity regimes or real deployment logs.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of any code release or reproducibility statement; while hyperparameters are reported, the LLM experiment details (prompt construction, judge prompting protocol, number of trials) are thin.

The paper does not include an explicit limitations section; the conditional nature of the gains and the heuristic delay analysis are only surfaced in the appendix rather than discussed candidly in the main text.
